title: Painter's Partition Problem
directAnswer: Each painter paints a contiguous block of boards, so the finishing time is the largest block-length sum across the k painters. Binary-search that answer: for a candidate time limit x, greedily assign boards left to right and count how many painters x forces. 'Can k painters finish if nobody works more than x?' is monotonic in x, so binary search finds the smallest feasible x in O(n log(sum)). Bounds are [max(board), sum(boards)].

remember.pattern: Binary search on the answer + greedy painter-count feasibility
remember.formula:
lo, hi = max(boards), sum(boards)
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if paintersNeeded(mid) <= k:   # painters required with time cap mid
        ans = mid; hi = mid - 1        # feasible → try a SMALLER time
    else:
        lo = mid + 1                   # infeasible → allow MORE time
rules: A painter paints a **contiguous** run of boards — that contiguity is what lets a single left-to-right sweep count the painters a time cap forces.
Lower bound is `max(board)`: whoever paints the longest single board needs at least that much time. Upper bound is `sum(boards)`: one painter does everything.
The predicate is **monotone increasing**: if a time cap `x` is enough, every cap `> x` is enough too. We MINIMIZE, so on a feasible mid go **left** (`hi = mid − 1`) and record it.
If boards have a per-unit time `t`, the answer is just `t ×` (min-max block sum) — fold `t` in at the end; it doesn't change the search.
Feasibility counts painters **forced** by the cap: open a new painter whenever the next board would push the running block past the cap. Bail early once the count exceeds k.
whenToUse: Workers/painters/machines each take a CONTIGUOUS slice of a sequence
You minimize the slowest worker's load — minimize the maximum block sum
A fast O(n) check answers 'how many workers does this load cap force?'
The answer is a number in [max(element), sum(elements)]
antiSignals: Painters can take non-contiguous boards → it's a scheduling/partition problem, not binary search on the answer
You must output the assignment, not just the finishing time → reconstruct after the search
Board lengths can be negative → running sums aren't monotone and the greedy count breaks
k is effectively unbounded → the answer is just max(board)
remember.takeaway: Painter's Partition is Allocate Pages wearing a different hat: minimize the largest contiguous block sum across k groups. Recognise the contiguous-split + min-max signature, bound the answer by [max, sum], binary-search it, and check feasibility with a one-pass greedy worker count. Same algorithm as Split Array Largest Sum.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize this as the same min-max-over-contiguous-groups problem as Allocate Pages, pin the answer bounds at [max(board), sum(boards)], and justify the monotone feasibility predicate before coding.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting the boards (which destroys contiguity), using lo = 0, or moving the search the wrong way on a feasible mid because the minimize/maximize direction got flipped.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it explicitly: 'this is Allocate Pages / Split Array Largest Sum'. State that feasible(time) is monotone increasing, justify lo = max(board), and fold any per-unit time factor in at the very end.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `boards` of `n` integers where `boards[i]` is the length of the i-th board, and an integer `k` — the number of painters.

Each painter paints a **contiguous** sequence of boards, painting 1 unit of board length takes 1 unit of time, and all painters work simultaneously.

Assign the boards so that the time to paint **all** boards is minimized. The total time is the time taken by the painter who finishes last (the largest block of lengths). Return that minimized time.
constraints: Painters work in parallel; a painter's time equals the sum of lengths in its contiguous block
If a per-unit time t is given, multiply the result by t
understanding: Cut the board array into k contiguous blocks and hand one block to each painter. Since they paint in parallel, the project finishes when the painter with the largest block finishes. You want the cut that minimizes that largest block sum — a single number, which is the binary-search-on-the-answer tell.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a painter skip around to non-adjacent boards?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — each painter's boards are contiguous. That's the whole reason a one-pass greedy count works.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do painters work in parallel or one after another?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In parallel. The finishing time is the maximum block sum, not the total. If it were sequential, the answer would just be sum(boards).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there a per-unit painting time?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If each unit length takes t time, solve for the min-max block sum first, then multiply by t at the end — it scales the answer linearly without changing the search.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why is the smallest possible time max(board)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Whoever paints the longest single board can't finish before that board is done, so no assignment beats max(board).

examples.explanation: Cut [10, 20, 30] | [40] → block sums 60 and 40 → the slower painter takes 60. Any other 2-way cut is worse (e.g. [10,20]|[30,40] → 70).
Cut [10, 10] | [10, 10] → both painters take 20. Balanced split, minimized maximum 20.
Cut [5, 10] | [30] | [20, 15] → sums 15, 30, 35 → slowest painter takes 35, the best achievable.

approaches.name: Linear Scan Over the Answer — Baseline
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this to show you've identified the search space (the finishing time) and the painter-count check. Then flag that the scan range is sum(boards), which is too big.
hints: The answer is some finishing time between max(boards) and sum(boards). What if you tried every time cap upward and returned the first that works?
For a fixed cap x, count painters: walk the boards, keep a running block sum, and start a new painter whenever the next board would push the block past x.
The first cap whose painter-count is ≤ k is the answer — and once a cap works, every larger cap works. But sum(boards) can be ~10⁹, so the scan dominates.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each candidate time (up to sum(boards)) runs an O(n) greedy painter count → O(n · sum). Fine for tiny totals, far too slow under the real constraints.
approaches.explanation:
Start with the reframing: you're choosing a *number* — the time the slowest painter is allowed to take — and that number lives in `[max(boards), sum(boards)]`. The lower end is `max(boards)` because whoever paints the longest board needs at least that long; the upper end is `sum(boards)` because a single painter could do every board.

**The feasibility check counts painters.** Fix a time cap `x`. Sweep the boards left to right with a running block sum. Add the current board; if that would exceed `x`, close the current painter's block and hand this board to a new painter. The painters opened is exactly the minimum needed under cap `x`, because the assignment is contiguous and lengths are non-negative — packing each painter as full as the cap allows minimizes how many painters you use.

**Why greedy-fill is exact.** Within a contiguous block the running sum only grows, and pushing a painter to work right up to the cap never forces *more* painters downstream — it can only leave less for later, which helps. So 'fill to the cap, then cut' yields the fewest painters for that cap — a precise yes/no feasibility answer, not an estimate.

**Why scanning upward is valid.** The first cap whose painter count is ≤ `k` is the minimum feasible time. Raising the cap only lets each painter absorb more boards, so it never increases the painter count — meaning once a cap works, all larger caps work. That 'larger cap ⇒ never worse' fact is the monotonicity we'll exploit next.

**Why we don't ship this.** `sum(boards)` can reach `10⁵ · 10⁴ = 10⁹`. An O(n) check run a billion times is hopeless. Because feasibility is monotone in the cap, binary-search the boundary instead of walking to it.
approaches.insight: The fact that 'a larger time cap never needs more painters' is precisely the proof that `feasible(x)` is monotone increasing — the green light to replace the linear scan with a binary search over the same candidate caps.

dryRun.intro: Caps start at max(boards)=40 and rise. For each, count painters greedily; return the first cap needing ≤ 2 painters.

approaches.name: Binary Search on the Finishing Time (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Phrase it as 'feasible(time) is monotone, so binary-search the smallest feasible finishing time'.
hints: You showed feasible(time) is false for small caps and true for large caps, flipping exactly once. What finds that flip in logarithmic time?
Binary-search the time cap in [max(boards), sum(boards)]. At each mid, run the O(n) greedy painter count. ≤ k painters means mid is feasible — record it and try smaller; otherwise try larger.
Because you MINIMIZE, on a feasible mid record ans = mid and move hi = mid - 1; on infeasible move lo = mid + 1. The last feasible mid is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The time range spans sum(boards), so binary search runs O(log(sum)) iterations, each doing the O(n) greedy count → O(n log(sum)). Computing bounds is O(n); space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
This is binary search on the answer, identical in structure to Allocate Pages — only the words 'students/pages' become 'painters/time'.

**The monotonic predicate, precisely.** Define `feasible(x) = true` if the boards split into at most `k` contiguous blocks each summing to ≤ `x`. Raising `x` never increases the painters forced (a roomier cap only lets each painter take more boards). So across `x` from `max(boards)` to `sum(boards)`, `feasible(x)` reads `[F, F, …, F, T, T, …, T]` — false while too tight, true once loose enough, flipping exactly once. **The answer is the smallest `x` that is true.**

**The feasibility check is the same painter count.** `paintersNeeded(x)` sweeps once, accumulating a block load and opening a new painter whenever the next board would push the load past `x`. Contiguity plus non-negative lengths make filling-to-the-cap the painter-minimizing strategy, so the count is exact — the hard requirement for binary-search-on-the-answer.

**Driving toward the smallest true.** Set `lo = max(boards)`, `hi = sum(boards)`. Compute `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`. If `paintersNeeded(mid) ≤ k`, `mid` works but a tighter cap might too — record `ans = mid` and search the lower half with `hi = mid − 1`. If `mid` needs more than `k` painters, it's too tight — search upward with `lo = mid + 1`. When `lo > hi`, `ans` holds the smallest feasible time.

**The off-by-one traps, named.** (1) `lo = 0` instead of `max(boards)` wastes iterations on caps that can't even hold the longest board. (2) Recording `ans` on the infeasible branch returns a time that doesn't actually fit `k` painters. (3) Flipping the direction — this is *minimize the maximum*, so a feasible mid means 'try smaller', i.e. move `hi` left. Going right returns a larger-than-necessary time. State the invariant 'ans is always a time that fits within k painters' and the moves follow.

**Folding in per-unit time.** If each unit length takes `t` time, the finishing time is `t ×` (min-max block sum). Solve the integer problem above, then multiply the result by `t` once at the end — the search itself is unchanged.
approaches.insight: Painter's Partition, Allocate Pages, and Split Array Largest Sum are the *same* algorithm; only the nouns differ. Once you can say 'minimize the maximum over a contiguous k-way split', you should write the [max, sum] binary search from muscle memory. The transferable skill is recognising that disguise, not re-deriving the search each time.

dryRun.intro: lo = max = 40, hi = sum = 100. Feasible mid → record and go left (minimize). ans tracks the smallest feasible time.

pitfalls: Setting lo = 0 instead of max(boards) — searches times that can't paint the longest board.
Recording ans on the infeasible branch — returns a time that needs more than k painters.
Going right on a feasible mid — that maximizes instead of minimizing.
Using (lo + hi) / 2 — overflows when sum approaches the int limit.

edgeCases.behavior: lo = hi = 100; the single painter takes 100 → answer 100.
One board each → slowest painter takes 1. lo = 1 is already feasible → answer 1.
One painter does everything → answer sum = 14, the upper bound.

commonMistakes: Sorting the boards — destroys the contiguity the problem requires.
Setting the lower bound to 0 instead of max(boards).
Moving hi/lo the wrong way on a feasible mid — minimize means go left.
Forgetting to multiply by the per-unit time t when the problem specifies one.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting the boards
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Painters take contiguous boards in the given order. Sorting reorders the line, so the blocks you count no longer correspond to valid assignments.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
Arrays.sort(boards);   // WRONG: contiguity is defined by original order
int lo = boards[boards.length - 1], hi = ...;
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int lo = 0, hi = 0;
for (int b : boards) { lo = Math.max(lo, b); hi += b; }  // no sort

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong lower bound
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The painter assigned the longest board can't finish before that board is done. Starting lo at 0 explores times that can never be feasible.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: lo, hi = 0, sum(boards)        # lo too low

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong direction on a feasible mid
commonMistakesDetailed.why: This minimizes the maximum, so a feasible time means 'a smaller time might also work'. Moving lo right returns a finishing time larger than the true minimum.
